claims.text: The selected HEA consists of multiple transition metals, exemplified by Nb, Ti, Zr, Hf, and Ta, in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios.
The constituent transition metals have partially filled d orbitals.
Electronic disorder and the resulting electron-phonon coupling strength primarily govern the emergence and strength of superconductivity.
Atomic-scale disorder and local chemical environments affect the alloy's electronic band structure and phonon modes.
Sufficient metallicity and a high density of states at the Fermi level permit superconductivity to emerge despite atomic disorder.
Superconductivity emerges when electron-phonon coupling is strong enough to enable Cooper-pair formation in the disordered alloy.
Excessive disorder can cause Anderson localization.
Excessive disorder can reduce the density of states at the Fermi level.
Excessive disorder or electronic localization suppresses superconductivity.
If superconductivity emerges, its critical temperature will be comparable to or lower than those of the constituent elements.
A superconducting transition will produce a sharp drop to zero electrical resistivity and a diamagnetic response.
The superconducting critical temperature is likely to lie between 1 K and 10 K.
If disorder dominates, no superconducting transition will be observed.
At room temperature, the alloy exhibits metallic behavior and no superconductivity.
The proposed mechanism applies to transition-metal HEAs that retain metallic conduction.
The proposed mechanism does not apply when strong localization, insulating behavior, or absent electron-phonon coupling occurs.
Unconventional pairing or magnetic impurities may complicate the proposed electron-phonon mechanism.
Failure to observe both zero resistivity and diamagnetism below 10 K would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis explicitly permits no superconducting transition when disorder/localization dominates, yet the falsification rule treats the absence of a transition below 10 K as falsifying the hypothesis. That null result is therefore compatible with one branch of the hypothesis and cannot decisively falsify it.
